name: Limnodea
look_here_first: OZARKGRASS: find a slender annual tuft with fibrous roots and a relatively NARROW, sometimes slightly nodding spring panicle. At 10–20× inspect ONE ~3–4 mm spikelet: TWO stiff nearly equal glumes enclose ONE fertile floret. The lemma has TWO small apical teeth; its SINGLE 8–12 mm often bent and twisted awn emerges BETWEEN those teeth. A true 1–2 mm membranous, minutely jagged ligule sits inside the blade–sheath junction. Flowerhead silhouette alone is not a confirmed ID; the current photo does NOT prove lemma teeth or ligule.

comparison_lesson.title: Ozarkgrass versus threeawns, lovegrasses, panicgrasses and muhlies
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: One fertile floret + 2 long nearly equal stiff glumes + 2 lemma-tip teeth framing ONE bent awn = Ozarkgrass candidate. Count actual florets and inspect the awn attachment.
quick_split: Aristida threeawns: normally THREE awn limbs arising from ONE lemma, vs Limnodea's single notched-lemma awn. Eragrostis lovegrasses: generally MULTIPLE florets per spikelet, not just one. Panicum (e.g., switchgrass): typically a lower sterile/staminate floret with a hardened fertile UPPER floret rather than one fertile floret with the Limnodea notched awn. Muhlenbergia: can ALSO have one fertile floret, so compare the paired glumes, lemma teeth/awn origin, ligule and annual tuft; panicle openness and one awn alone are insufficient.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Only one installed Limnodea species; no county-native inference, no imaginary micro-feature arrows.

rows: One fertile floret; 2 stiff subequal glumes; one bent awn from notch between 2 lemma teeth

what_to_teach_crew: OZARKGRASS: find a slender annual tuft with fibrous roots and a relatively NARROW, sometimes slightly nodding spring panicle. At 10–20× inspect ONE ~3–4 mm spikelet: TWO stiff nearly equal glumes enclose ONE fertile floret. The lemma has TWO small apical teeth; its SINGLE 8–12 mm often bent and twisted awn emerges BETWEEN those teeth. A true 1–2 mm membranous, minutely jagged ligule sits inside the blade–sheath junction. Flowerhead silhouette alone is not a confirmed ID; the current photo does NOT prove lemma teeth or ligule.

Aristida threeawns: normally THREE awn limbs arising from ONE lemma, vs Limnodea's single notched-lemma awn. Eragrostis lovegrasses: generally MULTIPLE florets per spikelet, not just one. Panicum (e.g., switchgrass): typically a lower sterile/staminate floret with a hardened fertile UPPER floret rather than one fertile floret with the Limnodea notched awn. Muhlenbergia: can ALSO have one fertile floret, so compare the paired glumes, lemma teeth/awn origin, ligule and annual tuft; panicle openness and one awn alone are insufficient.
Get same rooted plant, attached panicle, scaled mature spikelet and true 1–2-mm ligule closeup. Treat unresolved photos as genus-unknown grass.
visual_needs: WHOLE ROOTED PLANT: a connected fibrous-rooted tuft with entire narrow seedhead in frame and a 1-cm scale; no stolons or rhizomes.
WHOLE PANICLE: side view from flag leaf through narrowly ascending, sometimes nodding flowering branches with attached mature spikelets.
SPIKELET 10–20×: TWO stiff, subequal, ~3–4 mm glumes surrounding ONE fertile floret, mm ruler for scale.
CRITICAL LEMMA 20×: clearly show two terminal teeth and exactly ONE ~8–12 mm bent/twisted awn originating in notch BETWEEN those teeth.
LEAF COLLAR: turn back the blade and show the actual 1–2 mm ragged-edged membranous ligule with a 1-mm scale.
MATCHED LOOKALIKES: same-scale threeawn three-limbed lemma, lovegrass multifloret spikelet and panicgrass two-floret spikelet.

visual_comparison.title: Ozarkgrass — seven original Central Texas photo views, two new close-ups, and native-grass contrasts
visual_comparison.subtitle: Nine physically stored original species photographs (six credited Bob Harms; two CC BY detailed iNaturalist; one original CC BY-NC). Two new macro study panels show reproductive branches and collar. Still missing photographed actual 0.5mm two-toothed lemma tips and calibrated ligule.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: One fertile floret + 2 long nearly equal stiff glumes + 2 lemma-tip teeth framing ONE bent awn = Ozarkgrass candidate. Count actual florets and inspect the awn attachment.

items.label: 1 · TRUE OZARKGRASS — original field photograph
items.image_role: Existing original source-identified Limnodea photograph, with only gross flowering branch/spikelet arrows; not a confirmed microscope image of lemma or ligule.
items.caption: Existing real source-identified Ozarkgrass photo. Earlier two broad arrows remain attached to visible flowering branches and narrow spikelet units, not to microscopic anatomy. The whole panicle tends to be rather narrow; branch arching alone does not decide the species.
items.why_it_matters: A useful field candidate photo. The real split requires dissecting one mature spikelet to see the notched lemma with its single awn, two glumes and one floret.
items.creator: zcontreras
items.photo_status: Original species tag from source. Original licence and attribution retained; no inferred anatomy.

items.label: LEAF COLLAR MACRO — pale membrane region, exact free ligule not measured
items.image_role: Blade/sheath junction and pale collar tissue, but true free ligule edge unverified
items.caption: An original Ozarkgrass research-grade observation shows the blade passing into its enclosing sheath near a pale tissue projection. The leaf-collar junction is visible; without peeling the sheath fully open or a 1-mm ruler this does NOT prove the free ligule apex, membrane hairs, or ligule dimensions.
items.why_it_matters: Real observation-derived anatomy improves field teachability; do not misread hand scale as precise millimeter measurements.

items.label: 2 · PURPLE THREEAWN — OTHER species comparison
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.caption: This is purple THREEAWN, not Ozarkgrass. Aristida normally produces THREE awn limbs from one lemma; Limnodea has just one awn originating between two lemma-tip teeth.
items.why_it_matters: Count awns FROM ONE attached lemma, not awns scattered across an entire head.
items.image_role: Existing physically stored, source-attributed other-species comparison photograph (NOT Limnodea); no arrows to hidden structures
items.photo_status: Reused canonical existing other-species image; original media license/attribution preserved, not independently re-annotated.

items.label: 3 · SWITCHGRASS — OTHER species comparison
items.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
items.caption: This is SWITCHGRASS, not Ozarkgrass. Panicum has an upper fertile floret and usually a lower sterile/staminate floret; Limnodea has one fertile floret with the awn between two teeth at the lemma tip. This photo is NOT a dissected diagnostic Panicum spikelet.
items.why_it_matters: Panicle shape alone misleads; mature floret construction is the key.
